$comment: AUTHORITY for the surface of a Semiont client: every namespace, every method, the shape of what it returns, and what calling it does first. Every SDK is held to this table two ways. Its signatures are read by scripts/lint/check-client-surface.mjs, which fails on a method the table lacks, one an SDK lacks, and one whose return shape is not the row's; each of its sections holds the SDKs it has a reader for. Its behaviour is run: each SDK's surface test calls every method as each of its `cases` states and holds what the call did to the row. A method name is the table's, in camelCase; an SDK spells it by its language's convention (`resourceContent` is `resource_content` in Rust and `ResourceContent` in Go, whose first letter is a capital), and a namespace whose name is a keyword there takes a trailing underscore (`yield_`, `match_`). An `events` row is a property named `<method>$` in TypeScript. `absent` names an SDK that does not have the method, and why: the lint then fails if that SDK has it, so an exemption that stopped being true is caught. Add a row here before adding a method to any SDK. `worker` is the surface of what a worker is handed: the claims `job.claim` returns, and a job the worker holds. Each lists its members by name, and the same lint holds every SDK to the list both ways: a member the list has and an SDK lacks, and a public member an SDK has and the list lacks. A member is held by its name alone, spelled as its language spells it, and its form is its language's: what a held job states is a property in TypeScript and Python and a method in Rust, and a property that gives a stream of values is named `<member>$` in TypeScript. What a language's own protocols give a type is no member here: how a type is made, Python's names that begin with an underscore, its `__aenter__` and `__anext__` among them, Rust's trait implementations, and what a TypeScript class inherits from a class the SDK does not declare. `absent` is as it is for a method. `named` gives the name an SDK has the member under where its ecosystem has a name of its own for it, and why: the lint then fails if that SDK lacks that name, or has the table's name as well. `takes` marks a member a held job has as its verb's: for each verb, the schema of what the member takes. What a member does is not held here and these rows have no cases: docs/protocol/WORKER-CONTRACT.md states it, and the worker conformance suite (tests/conformance/worker) holds each SDK to it. Add a member here before adding it to any SDK. `stateUnits` lists each state unit: what each SDK makes it as (`made`), and its members by name. The same lint holds every SDK to it both ways: a unit an SDK does not declare, or declares as no `StateUnit`; a `StateUnit` an SDK declares among its units that no row makes; a member the list has and an SDK's unit lacks; and a public member an SDK's unit has and the list lacks. A member is held by its name alone, spelled as its language spells it, and its form is its language's, as for `worker`; a member's `absent` names an SDK whose unit has no such member, and why, and the lint then fails if that SDK's unit has it. `dispose` is no member here: every unit has it, being a `StateUnit`; nor is how a unit is made (a TypeScript class's constructor and its static factories among it). `absent` names an SDK that has no such unit, and why: the lint then fails if that SDK has one. What a unit does is not held here: each SDK's tests of its units hold that. Add a unit or a member here before adding it to any SDK. `wire` is the typed bus over a client's transport, which every client hands out as `wire`: what each SDK makes it as (`made`), and its members by name. The same lint holds every SDK to it both ways, as for a state unit: a bus an SDK does not declare, a member the list has and an SDK's bus lacks, and a public member an SDK's bus has and the list lacks; a member's `absent` names an SDK whose bus has no such member, and why, and the lint then fails if that SDK's has it. A member is held by its name alone, as for `worker`; how a bus is made is no member. A Go method takes no type parameters, so a member of Go's bus that is generic in its channel is a function of its package that takes the bus (`Emit(ctx, w, bus.MarkSubmit, payload)`). TypeScript's bus is read where @semiont/core declares it. A transport is no member: a bus hands out none. Add a member here before adding it to any SDK. `modules` is what each SDK has beside its namespaces: the free functions, types and values of its modules, each module with where each SDK keeps it and its members. A member is named as the table spells it and held by its `kind`: a `function` is spelled by each language's convention, a `reader` as a function but `get` and its name in TypeScript, a `type` as the table spells it, and a `constant` in capitals with underscores but in Go, as a function. `named` gives an SDK's own name where the rule does not, `absent` says why an SDK has none, and `notYetReached`, on a member or a module, names an SDK still to have it; each is stale, and fails the lint, once it is not so. A module whose `whole` names an SDK is that SDK's files alone, and every public member of them is listed.

shapes.promise: Asked once, answered once: the value, or a failure with a code.
shapes.stream: A long-running operation: what it reports as it goes, then its final value. Awaited, it gives the final value.
shapes.delegation: A job another party does: the job's events as it goes, the queue's naming of it the first of them and its completion the last. Awaited, it gives the completion.
shapes.upload: An upload in flight: its progress, then the id of the resource created.
shapes.cache: A live query. Building it touches nothing; its one-shot read asks the service now.
shapes.signal: Fire-and-forget. Nothing is returned and nothing is awaited.
shapes.count: A drive at the other participants: resolves with how many the gateway reached, or with no count when it kept none.
shapes.events: The events of one channel of the client's own bus, from now on.
shapes.claims: A worker's claims: each job it comes to hold, one at a time, from the first claim on. A held job starts, reports and settles itself.

via.request: A request of a bus operation, answered on its result or failure channel.
via.emit: A frame sent over the wire, with no reply awaited.
via.local: A frame published on the client's own bus and nowhere else.
via.content: An operation of the content transport: putBinary, getBinary, getBinaryStream, getResourceGraph, getAnnotations or getAnchoredText.
via.gateway: One of the gateway's own operations: getCurrentUser, getMediaToken, getProtectedResourceMetadata, healthCheck or getStatus.
via.observes: The channel of the client's own bus whose frames an `events` row gives.

worker.docs: What `job.claim` returns: each job the worker comes to hold, one at a time, and what the worker can say of itself meanwhile. How the jobs are read is the language's: subscribed to in TypeScript, iterated in Python, asked for one at a time in Rust, ranged over in Go.

absent.typescript: The claims are an rxjs Observable, read by subscribing to them: `subscribe` is rxjs's own, and the SDK declares no member for it.
absent.python: The claims are an asynchronous iterator, read with `async for`: `__anext__` is the language's protocol.

go.name: All
go.why: The claims are ranged over, `for job, err := range claims.All()`, and Go's standard library names the method that gives a sequence of every element `All` (`maps.All`, `slices.All`).

absent.rust: `next` answers a `Result`, and a claim that was refused is its `Err`: it is handed out where a job would be.
absent.python: The claims are iterated with `async for`, and an exception raised into the loop would end it; a claim that was refused does not end a worker's claims, so it is handed out where a job would be, as a `ClaimRefusal`.
absent.go: The claims are ranged over as pairs of a job and an error, and a claim that was refused is the error, a `*ClaimRefusal`: it is handed out where a job would be.

python.name: aclose
python.why: Python closes an asynchronous iterator with `aclose`: it is what an asynchronous generator has, and what `contextlib.aclosing` calls.

go.name: Close
go.why: Go stops what is held with `Close`, the name `io.Closer` gives it and what a `defer` calls.

worker.docs: A job a worker holds, from its claim until it settles it. A held job is its verb's, `mark` or `yield`. A member with `takes` is one a held job has as its verb's, and it takes what that verb's entry names; every other member is the same for both verbs, and a job held as either verb's has it without its verb being asked.

absent.rust: `complete`, `fail` and `cancel` take the job by value: a job its holder has settled is gone, and nothing is left to ask it.

stateUnits.docs: What a host shows about a session, apart from the session: that it ended and why, that a request was refused for lack of permission, and that a different knowledge base answers at a registered address. Each is a notice while something is raised and none once it is acknowledged; raising it again is a new occurrence, told to every reader even when the notice equals the last. A host builds one beside each live session and wires the session's failures into it.

stateUnits.docs: Values the knowledge base answers with, kept by key and held as state: each key's state (pending, ready with its value, or failed), fetched when first observed and again when invalidated, and set, removed or invalidated by its methods. stateUnits.docs: A session with one knowledge base: the token its client's transport sends and who is signed in, the token renewed before it expires and when the gateway refuses it. It writes its token and who is signed in, so it ends them; it only uses its client, so it never ends it, and whoever made the client and the session ends both. What it does is held by the session's own table (specs/src/session/cases.json), not by the behaviour table.

wire.docs: The typed bus over a client's transport, which a client hands out as `wire`: what it emits goes over the wire, and what it reads is what the wire delivers. A read gives each frame with its envelope, who emitted it and the trace it was sent under. A channel of a resource's scope is read for one resource, and the read holds that resource's scope while it is read. The client's own in-process signals are on its own bus, never here. It hands out no transport: a client's transport is the client's `transport`, and only there.
